Let’s dive into Chapter 3: Streamlining Preparation and Embracing Shortcuts.
You know, time is probably the most precious ingredient when it comes to cooking at home. The real difference between a dinner that feels totally doable and one that just overwhelms you? It usually comes down to how you prep. If you can streamline both your planning and your actual cooking, suddenly making a good meal—even on the busiest days—feels a whole lot easier.
One of the best things you can do is embrace shortcuts—without a hint of guilt. Think about those ready-prepped ingredients: pre-washed salad greens, chopped veggies, maybe even a rotisserie chicken from the store. These aren’t cheating. They’re just smart ways to bring fresh, wholesome food to the table fast. You don’t have to make everything from scratch every time. The real goal is to use what’s available in a way that works for you.
Here’s another trick: simplify the cooking itself. So many delicious dishes can be made in just one pan or one pot. That means less prep, and—maybe best of all—less cleanup. Imagine tossing some vegetables and chicken onto a baking tray, sliding it into the oven, and having dinner ready in under an hour. Or making a one-pot pasta where all the ingredients cook together and share their flavors. It saves time, sure, but it also makes everything taste richer.
Efficient kitchen organization is a secret weapon here, too. Keep your knives sharp, have your favorite utensils close by, and try to keep those counters clear. When you set out all your ingredients before you start—what chefs call “mise en place”—you can move from step to step without stopping to hunt for something you need. No more last-minute scrambles or forgotten ingredients.
And if you can plan ahead, even just a little, it really pays off. Maybe you cook a little extra so tomorrow’s lunch is already sorted. Or you chop extra veggies on Sunday to use during the week. Marinating meat the night before? That’s a tiny bit of effort for a big reward later. These habits don’t need complicated schedules—just a bit of planning and flexibility.
Here are a few practical techniques to make prep even easier:
Use kitchen scissors to snip herbs, slice bacon, or even cut up a pizza in seconds.
Grate garlic or ginger straight into your pan—no need to chop.
Cook double batches of things like grains or sauces, so you’ve got them on hand all week.
And don’t forget—embracing imperfection is part of the process. Not every meal is going to look like a magazine cover, and that’s totally fine. Focus on great flavors and nourishing yourself and your family. If things don’t go exactly to plan, that’s okay. By letting go of those unrealistic expectations, you’ll actually enjoy cooking—and eating—even more.
So, here’s the big takeaway: streamlining preparation is about making cooking fit into your real life, not the other way around. When you use shortcuts, simplify your steps, and plan ahead just a little, you can sit down to good food every day—no matter how hectic your schedule gets.
